extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, employers, employment lawyers, labor economists, and public commenters on FTC non‑compete rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether employer-imposed non-compete clauses constitute unfair methods of competition under Section 5 of the FTC Act, using legal standard, empirical studies, and public comment evidence about effects on labor mobility, earnings, job quality, and competitive conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitative and coercive nature of non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that non-competes "are exploitative and coercive because they trap workers in jobs or force them to bear significant harms and costs," particularly for workers other than senior executives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidence that workers abide by non-competes even when they believe them unenforceable; fear of litigation and legal fees; threats of litigation; attorneys' fee-shifting provisions or forced arbitration; compensation clawbacks; reputation harms; and examples across both lower- and high-wage industries. Note Commission's finding that mere existence of compensation does not automatically make the non-compete fair and that workers rarely bargain for non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions (legal standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Section 5, an unfair method of competition requires only a 'tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions' rather than proof of direct causation in a specific instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether non-competes, by their nature and aggregate operation, tend to impair competition in labor markets (e.g., by inhibiting efficient matching between workers and employers) even if the impact of any single non-compete is marginal or statistically indiscernible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-competes inhibit efficient matching and reduce competition for labor
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes introduce frictions that inhibit efficient matching between workers and employers by preventing workers from accepting better jobs within the scope (or perceived scope) of the non-compete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether non-competes reduce the number of competing options for workers and employers, diminish voluntary labor mobility, and thereby undercut the competitive process that sets wages and working conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of labor mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence and comments show non-competes reduce rates of job separations, hiring, job-to-job mobility, implicit mobility (tenure), and within- and between-industry mobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh studies that measure changes in enforceability (e.g., Johnson, Lavetti, and Lipsitz; Starr; Balasubramanian et al.; Lipsitz and Starr) showing increases in mobility when enforceability decreases; account for scope limitations of studies (industry-specific, geographic, sample). Give weight to consistent findings across methodologies and to qualitative comments reporting restricted mobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: In terrorem (chilling) effect even when unenforceable
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes can have a powerful 'in terrorem' effect because workers' belief about the likelihood of enforcement deters mobility even where State law would likely render a non-compete unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess workers' perceptions and evidence that litigation costs, uncertainty, and employer advantages deter challenges; consider that the mere existence of a non-compete may prevent switching jobs or starting businesses, supporting the need for clear federal notice or prohibition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suppression of workers' earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes tend to suppress workers' earnings across the labor market and for specific worker groups, in part because they reduce labor mobility and job offer rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider empirical estimates (e.g., nationwide ban estimated to increase earnings by ~3-14% per Johnson et al.; state-level estimates: Oregon ban 2-3%/4.6% in certain occupations; Hawaii ban ~4% for new hires), studies showing effects on responsiveness to labor market conditions, and evidence that non-competes increase racial and gender wage gaps. Account for stronger causal evidence from studies using legal changes in enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spillover and market-wide effects (including bordering states and workers without non-competes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes affect not only workers subject to them but also broader labor markets and workers without non-competes, including measurable cross-border effects where one State's enforceability changes affect neighboring States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate studies that identify spillovers (e.g., Johnson et al. finding border-state effects ~76% of direct effect; Starr, Frake, and Agarwal finding lower job-offer rates in high-use State/industry combinations), and consider how industry/state prevalence shapes broader market outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction in job quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative evidence indicates non-competes reduce job quality, which bolsters findings about negative effects on competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include commenters' reports of diminished job satisfaction, reduced raises/promotions, longer commutes, forced career changes, and other non-wage harms when assessing non-competes' effects on competitive conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential vulnerability by occupation, specialization, and licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly trained, specialized, or licensed workers (e.g., physicians) and workers with high student loan debt face heightened challenges from non-competes, making relocation or alternative employment more difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how occupational specialization, licensing requirements, credentialing, and debt burdens constrain alternative employment options and amplify coercive and anticompetitive effects, even for high-wage workers in small or niche fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological weighting of empirical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that examine changes in non-compete enforceability (natural experiments, legal changes) are generally more credible for causal inference than studies that merely correlate non-compete use with outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greater weight to longitudinal or quasi-experimental designs (e.g., pre/post law changes, interstate comparisons with appropriate counterfactuals). Treat cross-sectional associations of 'use' as less informative and give them minimal weight unless mitigated by stronger identification strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of commenters' qualitative evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Large numbers of individual and organizational comments describing personal experiences and harms can corroborate and bolster empirical findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat consistent, widespread qualitative reports—thousands of commenters reporting limited mobility, suppressed earnings, threats, and litigation fears—as supporting evidence alongside empirical studies, particularly where they align with quantitative results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer litigation advantages and procedural barriers as part of coercion analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers' advantages—deeper pockets, greater access to counsel, ability to deduct litigation costs, attorneys' fee-shifting clauses, forced arbitration, and reputational leverage—make workers reluctant to challenge non-competes and increase coercive effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate contract terms and litigation/ADR procedures that increase the expected cost of challenging non-competes, and consider how these procedural features magnify the practical enforceability and chilling effect of otherwise unenforceable clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation or bargaining at contracting does not conclusively justify non-competes
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that non-competes are fair if 'bargained for and fairly compensated' are undermined by record evidence that workers rarely bargain and compensation does not automatically make the restriction fair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether there was real bargaining power, adequate and fair compensation, and whether compensation made the restriction non-exploitative; plain existence of some compensation or bundling with equity/severance is not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and aggregate harm consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Because non-competes are prevalent across the U.S. labor force, aggregate effects across many contracts support a finding of harm to competitive conditions even if the impact of any single contract is small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prevalence data and aggregate empirical findings to determine market-level impact, recognizing that legal standard requires a tendency to harm rather than proof of isolated, case-specific harm.
